hints: Use two indices, one starting at each end of the string.
Move the left index forward until it points to a vowel, and move the right index backward until it points to a vowel.
When both indices point to vowels, swap them and move both inward.
Remember to treat A, E, I, O, and U as vowels too.
title: Invert Vowels of a String

notes: Only the vowels a, e, i, o, u and their uppercase forms are reversed. Every consonant, digit, space, and punctuation character remains at its original position.
constraints: s consists of printable ASCII characters.
content.inputFormat: Single line: JSON array of all arguments, e.g. [arg1, arg2, ...]

sampleTestCases.explanation: The vowels are I, e, e, A. Reversing their order gives A, e, e, I while all other characters stay fixed.
The vowels e, e, o, e are reversed to e, o, e, e, producing leotcede.

content.problemStatement:
With a string `s`, reverse only all the vowels in the string and output it.

The vowels are `'a'`, `'e'`, `'i'`, `'o'`, and `'u'`, and they can appear in both lower and upper cases, more than once.

**Example 1:**

**Input:** s = "IceCreAm"

**Output:** "AceCreIm"

**Explanation:**

The vowels in `s` are `['I', 'e', 'e', 'A']`. On reversing the vowels, s becomes `"AceCreIm"`.

**Example 2:**

**Input:** s = "leetcode"

**Output:** "leotcede"

**Constraints:**

* `1 <= s.length <= 21 * 10^5`
* `s` consist of **printable ASCII** characters.

notes: Solutions must preserve every non-vowel character exactly and reverse only ASCII vowels.
The vowel test must include both lowercase and uppercase ASCII vowels.
Each character is examined a constant number of times.
solution.approach: Use two pointers at the left and right ends. Advance the left pointer until it reaches a vowel and move the right pointer backward until it reaches a vowel. When both pointers are on vowels, swap them and continue inward. A mutable character buffer is used because the input string itself is immutable in several supported languages.

better.complexity: O(n) time and O(k) extra space for vowel positions/values.
better.description: Record the positions of all vowels, reverse the vowel values, and write them back to those positions. This is simpler to reason about than nested searches but still requires storing every vowel position.

optimal.complexity: O(n) time and O(n) total space for the mutable result buffer; O(1) auxiliary space.
optimal.description: Use two pointers and swap vowels directly from opposite ends. The pointers skip non-vowels, so every swap places the correct pair of vowels without storing their positions.

bruteForce.complexity: O(n) time and O(k) extra space for k vowels, in addition to the output buffer.
bruteForce.description: Scan the string to collect all vowels in order, reverse the collected list, then scan the original string again and replace each vowel with the next value from the reversed list.

solution.timeComplexity: O(n), where n is the length of s.
solution.spaceComplexity: O(n) total space for the mutable result buffer; O(1) auxiliary space beyond that buffer.

followUps: Can you implement the solution with O(1) auxiliary space beyond the character buffer?
Can you write the two-pointer scan iteratively without collecting vowel positions?
How would the approach change if the definition of a vowel were configurable at runtime?
learningObjectives: Apply the two-pointer technique to strings.
Distinguish characters that should move from characters that must remain fixed.
Handle uppercase and lowercase ASCII characters correctly.
Analyze linear-time string algorithms and auxiliary space usage.
